newsitem.title: USA: U.S. core CPI may hold key to next Fed move - source.
newsitem.headline: U.S. core CPI may hold key to next Fed move - source.

text.p: - The performance of the U.S. core Consumer Price Index will likely be the decisive factor as the Federal Reserve meets to set monetary policy in two weeks, a Fed source said.
"The Fed won't wait (to raise rates) if the data show we can't afford to wait," the source told Reuters in an interview conducted after Friday's release of the August employment report.
"The core CPI is not the only inflation number we look at, but it is the most visible," the source added.
The August CPI report is due out on Friday. A Reuter survey predicts CPI rose 0.2 percent, either including or excluding relatively volatile food and energy prices.
"Overall, the core has behaved well. There is no reason for alarm," the source also noted, referring to the 2.7-percent year-over-year core CPI increase.
The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee next meets on September 24.
The source said the economy appears to have little room left to grow at current rates without sparking inflation.

As evidence of dwindling slack in the economy, he cited a report last Friday showing U.S. unemployment fell to 5.1 percent in August amid strong payroll creation. But he noted the seven-year low unemployment rate may reflect special factors and does not necessarily indicate a new trend.
The source also noted the current expansion is marked by fierce competition for market share, keeping a lid on prices.

"One factor people forget is that market rates, like the (federal) funds rate, operate with a lag. Market rates started rising last spring, meaning we won't really see an effect until the fourth quarter," the source added.
The Fed has been banking on an economic slowdown to prevent the overheating of the economy.
The source also noted the Fed has historically tended to "overshoot," or raise and lower rates too much in any given cycle -- a mistake it now seeks to avoid.
The last Fed funds rate cut to 5.25 percent from 5.50 percent is an example of such an overshoot, the source said.
"The January easing was a mistake," he added.
Several transitory factors dampening growth last winter -- severe weather, government furloughs and strikes in the private sector -- clouded the Fed's economic view, he said.

The source added the Fed is hopeful for evidence the economy can continue growing without faster inflation due to corporate restructuring, leaner worker compensations, massive business investments and new technology.
This would indicate higher productivity, a measure particularly difficult to evaluate in an economy heavily weighted toward the service sector.
"We are looking for persuasive evidence," he added, in reference to inflation.
The source stressed the Fed sees the 5.25-percent federal funds rate as "still slightly restrictive in real terms."
Based on core CPI inflation at 2.7 percent, the real funds rate is at 250 basis points -- or about 25 to 50 basis points above its historic average.
The source also said there is a "unanimity" within the FOMC regarding the issue of long-term price stability.
"It's the long-term goal. Long-term is the key word," the source stressed. "You have to evaluate the cost (to the economy) of achieving price stability."

The source also said the consensus within the Fed is that "price stability is somewhere below 2.0 percent (core CPI)" but reaching that target in the near-term would mean implementing a monetary policy so restrictive that it would greatly heighten the risks of a recession.

"It's a long-toothed expansion," the source concluded, adding business investments are likely to slow down and the consumer to switch spending "to non-durable goods and services, since pent-up demand (for big-ticket items) has been met."
